A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICLR review-evaluation research despite the changed title and framing. All 25 pages of v2 and 27 pages of v4, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of eight LLMs, annotation reliability, agreement with expert reviews, focus distributions and rejection rates, with detailed appendix results.

after.justification: v4 retains original model and annotation evaluations and adds results for fine-tuned GPT-4o, MARG and accepted papers.

M1.justification: v4 implements supervised fine-tuning of GPT-4o on the paper-review corpus (Appendix A.3), whereas v2 only suggests fine-tuning as future work. The core extraction chain, annotation prompts, target/aspect categories and o3-mini annotator remain unchanged; the focus terminology largely reframes existing distribution analysis.

E1.justification: v4 adds evaluation on 40 accepted papers, extending the previously rejected-paper-only population. It also removes the final-decision accuracy evaluation reported in v2, although the retained generation prompt still requests an acceptance recommendation. These changes alter both population and evaluated task coverage within the same ICLR domain.

E2.justification: Table 3 and Figure 4 add MARG and fine-tuned GPT-4o to the eight retained off-the-shelf LLMs, broadening comparison to specialized review generation and task-specific training. MARG was previously only cited and is now evaluated for weaknesses.

E3.justification: v4 adds KL divergence and ROUGE-L, BERTScore and BLEU-4, while removing rejection-rate evaluation. New protocols include a 582-training/98-test fine-tuning split with five token-limit exclusions, timestamp-based selection of submitted versions for accepted papers, and weakness-only scoring for MARG. Whether all Table 3 models use the same test subset is unclear.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a targeted check of whether focus biases persist on accepted papers. The fine-tuning comparison also tests a mitigation suggested in v2. Existing annotation confusion matrices and discrepancy examples remain unchanged, and no extensive component-ablation study is added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or sampling-uncertainty estimates. The revised annotation-agreement values remain point estimates.

E6.justification: Table 3 adds similarity metrics and comparator results, including fine-tuned GPT-4o's KL divergence of 0.022 and MARG's weakness F1 of 0.346; Figure 17 adds accepted-paper findings. Table 2 changes o3-mini agreement from 0.85/0.86 to 0.81/0.79, and GPT-4o's overall F1 changes from 0.349 to 0.348. Rejection results and pair-level precision/recall columns disappear. Detailed appendix Tables 7–12 retain their values.

T1.justification: v4's E(L,A,P) and positive/negative focus-vector notation formalizes the normalized facet-frequency distributions already examined in v2 Figure 4 without changing their mathematical substance. No substantive assumptions, derivations, formal properties or proofs are added.

C1.justification: v4 centers the contribution on a distinct focus-level evaluation framework and removes the core claim about inaccurate acceptance decisions. It adds claims about fine-tuning producing the closest focus distributions and different models excelling under different metrics. The technical-validity bias and neglected-novelty findings are retained, with qualifications for untuned models.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations concerning complementary human/LLM reviewer roles, metric-dependent strengths, focus-based training objectives and applicability beyond paper reviewing. It emphasizes that fine-tuning can improve aggregate focus while review-point agreement remains low. The earlier discussion of consistency between review points and final decisions is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds the fine-tuning API, data split, token exclusions and settings of four epochs, batch size four and learning-rate multiplier 0.1. v4 also specifies annotator expertise and Cohen's kappa. Conversely, v2's explicit extraction-model and default-parameter disclosures disappear. The release description changes from 68 to 676 papers at the same dataset link, without establishing changed availability.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially repositions the contribution as focus-level evaluation complementing surface-, content- and decision-level assessments. Added references support facet analysis, holistic evaluation and multi-objective training, including Lu et al. (2025), Liang et al. (2022), Yang et al. (2024) and Agnihotri et al. (2025). Much of the existing related-work discussion remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around review focus. Section 2 replaces the short task description with a framework explanation, Sections 4–5 are reorganized, and the discussion is extensively revised. Appendix sections are reorganized to accommodate facet definitions, fine-tuning details and accepted-paper results.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redesigned, Figure 4 replaces overlapping radar plots with labeled stacked bars, and Table 3 receives new metric groups, comparator rows and highlighting. The codebook moves to the appendix with a compact main-text replacement. The rejection table and redundant F1 summary disappear; a hyperparameter table and accepted-paper figure are added.

improvement.justification: v4 more clearly distinguishes aggregate review focus from agreement on individual review points, supported by the complementary metrics in Table 3 and clearer figures. The accepted-paper check partially addresses v2's restricted evaluation population. These gains are limited by unclear test-set comparability for fine-tuned GPT-4o and the loss of some implementation disclosures. The evidence supports a modest net improvement in clarity and empirical support.
